summary: This best current practice describes a simple process in which authors of Internet-Drafts add an Implementation Status section recording known implementations. That lets reviewers and working groups give proper weight to documents backed by running code, which can be evidence that a specification works.

plainLanguage.summary: This document suggests a way for the author of an Internet-Draft to say which implementations of the protocol already exist, and to say how complete and mature they are. The idea is that a reviewer can then judge the specification against code that runs, and that problems in the specification show up early, while it is still a draft.

questions: what is the implementation status section
what is rough consensus and running code
is the implementation status section mandatory
subtitle: How an Internet-Draft can list known implementations, and why the IETF thinks running code is worth recording.

tldr.problem: Implementation is not required before a protocol specification is published as an RFC, so a document can reach Proposed Standard with no code behind it and some may never be implemented.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes an optional Implementation Status section for Internet-Drafts, listing for each known implementation who wrote it, how mature it is, which parts of the specification it covers, its licence and its contact details.
tldr.outcome: Working groups and reviewers can give documents with running code due consideration, and the section is meant to be removed before publication so that its time-dependent content does not have to be maintained afterwards. The RFC obsoletes RFC 6982 and advances the experiment to Best Current Practice.

facts.label: Where the section goes
facts.value: Just before the Security Considerations section

facts.label: Maturity levels named
facts.value: research, prototype, alpha, beta, production, widely used

today: RFC 7942 is a Best Current Practice published in July 2016. It advances the experiment started in RFC 6982, which it obsoletes, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Running Code Matters
sections.content:
Most IETF participants are familiar with the saying rough consensus and running code and can identify with its pragmatic approach. However, implementation is not a requirement for publication as an RFC. There are many examples of Internet-Drafts containing protocol specifications that went through to publication as Proposed Standard RFCs without implementation, and some of them may never get implemented.

Over time, a variety of policies have been applied within the IETF to consider running code. In the Routing Area it used to be a requirement that one or more implementations must exist before an Internet-Draft could be published as a Proposed Standard RFC. That requirement was later lifted, but each working group was given the authority to impose its own implementation requirements, and at least one working group, Inter-Domain Routing, continues to require two independent implementations.

The hypothesis behind the document is that there are benefits to the IETF standardization process in producing implementations of protocol specifications before publication as RFCs. These benefits include determining that the specification is comprehensible and that there is sufficient interest to implement it.

The document describes a simple mechanism that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record and publicize the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. It defines, quite informally, the contents of this section to ensure that the relevant information is included. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

It is up to the individual working groups to use this information as they see fit, but one result might be the preferential treatment of documents, resulting in them being processed more rapidly. The document recommends that the Implementation Status section should be removed from Internet-Drafts before they are published as RFCs. As a result, no changes to the section are envisaged after approval of the document for publication, and the RFC errata process does not apply.

The process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using it, and working groups are invited to think about applying it to all of their protocol specifications. Its scope is all Internet-Drafts that contain implementable specifications, whether produced within IETF working groups or outside working groups but intended for IETF consensus. Internet-Drafts published on the Independent Stream are explicitly out of scope, and it is expected that the greatest benefit will be seen with Standards Track documents developed within working groups.

The process was initially proposed as an experiment in RFC 6982, which is now obsoleted, and the process advanced to Best Current Practice. Historically there have been other ways for experience based on protocol implementations to feed back into the IETF process: many implementation reports have been published, in some cases several years after the protocol was originally published. Providing feedback to published protocols is a related goal, but different from this document's focus.
sections.plainLanguage: A specification can reach the RFC stage without any code behind it. This document asks authors to list the code that does exist, so that reviewers can see whether the specification is understandable and workable in practice.

sections.title: The Implementation Status Section
sections.content:
Each Internet-Draft may contain a section entitled Implementation Status. This section, if it appears, should be located just before the Security Considerations section, and should contain, for each existing implementation, some or all of the following:

  • The organization responsible for the implementation, if any.
  • The implementation's name and/or a link to a web page where the implementation or a description of it can be found.
  • A brief general description.
  • The implementation's level of maturity: research, prototype, alpha, beta, production, widely used, and so on.
  • Coverage: which parts of the protocol specification are implemented.
  • Version compatibility: what version or versions of the Internet-Draft are known to be implemented.
  • Licensing: the terms under which the implementation can be used, for example proprietary, royalty licensing, freely distributable with acknowledgement (BSD style), freely distributable with a requirement to redistribute source (General Public License style), and other (specify).
  • Implementation experience: any useful information the implementers want to share with the community.
  • Contact information: ideally a person's name and email address, but possibly just a URL or mailing list.
  • The date when information about this particular implementation was last updated.

In addition, the section can contain information about the interoperability of any or all of the implementations, including references to test-case descriptions and interoperability reports, when such exist.

Working group chairs and area directors are requested to ensure that this section is not used as a marketing venue for specific implementations. Since the information is necessarily time dependent, it is inappropriate for inclusion in a published RFC, and the authors should include a note to the RFC Editor requesting that the section be removed before publication.
sections.plainLanguage: The Implementation Status section goes just before the security section of the draft, and it lists, for each implementation, who wrote it, how finished it is, which parts of the specification it covers, which draft version it follows, and how it may be used. It is meant to be removed when the draft becomes an RFC, because the facts in it go out of date.

sections.title: The Boilerplate Text
sections.content:
The document proposes the following boilerplate text to head the Implementation Status section, and asks authors to add a note to the RFC Editor at the top of the section advising the Editor to remove the entire section before publication, as well as the reference to RFC 7942.

This section records the status of known implementations of the protocol defined by this specification at the time of posting of this Internet-Draft, and is based on a proposal described in RFC 7942. The description of implementations in this section is intended to assist the IETF in its decision processes in progressing drafts to RFCs. Please note that the listing of any individual implementation here does not imply endorsement by the IETF. Furthermore, no effort has been spent to verify the information presented here that was supplied by IETF contributors. This is not intended as, and must not be construed to be, a catalog of available implementations or their features. Readers are advised to note that other implementations may exist.
sections.plainLanguage: A fixed paragraph goes at the top of the section, so that every draft says the same thing about what the list means: it is not an endorsement, nobody has checked the entries, and there may be implementations that are not listed.

sections.title: Publishing the List Separately
sections.content:
Sometimes it can be advantageous to publish the implementation status separately from the base Internet-Draft, for example on the IETF wiki:

  • When the Implementation Status section becomes too large to be conveniently managed within the document.
  • When a working group decides to have implementors, rather than authors, keep the status of their implementations current.
  • When a working group already maintains an active wiki and prefers to use it for this purpose.
  • If the working group decides that the information is still valuable, and needs to be kept current, after the draft is published as an RFC and the Implementation Status section has been removed from it.

It is highly desirable for all readers of the Internet-Draft to be made aware of this information. Initially this can be done by replacing the Implementation Status section's contents with a URL pointing to the wiki. Later, the IETF Tools may support this functionality, for example by including such a link in the HTML file of the document, similar to the IPR link.

If the implementation status is published separately from the draft, then this information needs to be openly available without requiring authentication, registration or access controls, if it is to have any useful effects.
sections.plainLanguage: The list can live on a wiki instead of in the draft, which is useful when implementers keep it up to date themselves. If it does, the draft should still point to it, and the wiki must be readable by anyone, with no login.

sections.title: The Benefits
sections.content:
Publishing the information about implementations provides the working group with several benefits:

  • Working group members, chairs and area directors may use the information to help prioritize the progress of drafts, for example when there are several competing proposals to solve a particular problem.
  • Similarly, the information is useful when deciding whether the document should be progressed on a different track, such as an individual submission or Experimental.
  • Making the information public and an explicit part of working group deliberations will motivate participants to implement protocol proposals, which in turn helps in discovering protocol flaws at an early stage.
  • Other participants can use the software to evaluate the usefulness of protocol features, its correctness to some degree, and other properties such as resilience and scalability.
  • Working group members may choose to perform interoperability testing with known implementations, especially when they are publicly available.
  • In the case of open source, people may want to study the code to better understand the protocol and its limitations, determine if the implementation matches the protocol specification, and whether the protocol specification has omissions or ambiguities.
  • Some protocol features may be hard to understand, and for such features the mere assurance that they can be implemented is beneficial. The document notes though that code should never be used in lieu of a clear specification.

The document does not specify whether, or to what degree, working groups are expected to prefer proposals that have running code associated with them over others that do not. Working group chairs are invited to suggest this mechanism to document editors in their working groups, and to draw the attention of their working group participants to Implementation Status sections where they exist.
sections.plainLanguage: Listing the code gives a working group something concrete to weigh: it can see which parts of the design are already understood well enough to build, test against, and find the gaps in. The document stops short of saying that a working group should prefer a proposal because code exists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document says that it is a process document, and therefore does not have a direct effect on the security of any particular IETF protocol. However, better-reviewed protocols are likely to also be more secure.

The document has no IANA actions of its own, since it defines no new registry. Its effects are on the way drafts are written: the Implementation Status section is recommended for removal before publication, so that the RFC itself does not carry time-dependent claims.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes any protocol, so it has no direct security effect. The argument is indirect: a protocol that has been built and tested is likely to be a better and safer protocol.

viz.caption: WHAT AN IMPLEMENTATION ENTRY MAY CONTAIN

items.title: Organization
items.text: Who is responsible for the implementation, if anyone.

items.title: Name and link
items.text: The implementation's name, or a page describing it.

items.title: Description
items.text: A brief general description of what it is.

items.title: Maturity
items.text: Research, prototype, alpha, beta, production, widely used.

items.title: Coverage
items.text: Which parts of the protocol specification are implemented.

items.title: Version compatibility
items.text: Which versions of the draft are known to be implemented.

items.title: Licensing
items.text: Proprietary, royalty licensing, freely distributable with acknowledgement, freely distributable with source redistribution, or other.

items.title: Contact and date
items.text: Who to ask about it, and when the entry was last updated.

viz.caption: WHEN TO PUBLISH THE LIST SOMEWHERE ELSE

items.title: The section is too large
items.text: It has become unwieldy inside the draft.

items.title: Implementers maintain it
items.text: A working group decides implementors, not authors, keep the list current.

items.title: A wiki already exists
items.text: The working group keeps an active wiki and prefers to use it.

items.title: It outlives the draft
items.text: The information is still worth keeping after the draft is published and the section removed.

items.title: Prioritizing drafts
items.text: Working groups can weigh competing proposals against something concrete.

items.title: Choosing a track
items.text: The information helps decide whether a document should go a different way.

items.title: Finding flaws early
items.text: Implementing a proposal is how protocol flaws turn up before publication.

items.title: Checking the specification
items.text: Code shows whether the features are useful, correct, resilient and scalable.

items.title: Interoperability testing
items.text: Known implementations give working groups something to test against.

items.title: Studying the code
items.text: Reading an implementation shows omissions and ambiguities in the specification.
